Definition / Scope Note: Korean independence activist (1902-1920). Arrested during March 1st Movement, died in Seodaemun Prison age 17. Central figure in 'exchangeable identity' strategy: 'Her identity... exchangeable with any other heroine in history.' (p.30)

French martyr (1412-1431). Postcolonial parallel to Yu Gwan-sun: both young women martyred by imperial powers. Incantatory invocation p.28: 'She calls the name Jeanne d'Arc three times.' Also appears through Thérèse's performance and Falconetti's portrayal.

Carmelite nun (1873-1897). Author of Story of a Soul. Shares name 'Theresa' with Cha (Catholic baptismal name from Sacred Heart Convent). Performs as Joan of Arc in 1895 play. Right-page narrative in ERATO split-screen structure.
Last Empress of Korea (1851-1895). Assassination date deliberately altered to 1919 in text — intentional temporal collapse to show colonial violence as recurring structure, not sequential events.
French actress (1892-1946). Portrays Joan of Arc in Dreyer's silent film La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc (1928). Silent woman in silent medium — visual signifier of foreclosed speech throughout ERATO.

Cha's mother (b.1922 Yongjing, Manchuria). Triple-language speaker under colonial rule: Korean forbidden, Japanese enforced, Chinese ambient. Embodies intergenerational translational violence. Fictional letter form in CALLIOPE. Portrait p.44 also used in Cha's 1977 video Chronology.

Cha's father. Calligrapher. His brush calligraphy 女男 (pp.26-27), 父母 (pp.54-55) placed at center of pages. Daoist cosmological concepts in TERPSICHORE (p.154). Cantonese pronunciation transcription in POLYMNIA (p.173).

Cha's older brother. Participated in April 19 Revolution demonstrations. Tutor's warning: 'they are killing any student in uniform' (p.84). Family's subsequent exile to US motivated by his political activity. 'De.Mo' syllabic split = democracy decomposed.

French: female monologue performer. Cha's textual shaman who empties self to channel 9 Muses: 'She allows others. In place of her. Admits others to make full.' (p.3). Not fluent speaker but medium of fragments: 'noise, groan, bits torn from words.' Takes on punctuation as bodily condition: 'She would become, herself, demarcations.' (p.4). Structural frame for entire work. NOTE: Treated as distinct entity from Cha — conflation refused at data level.

Korean shamanic origin myth: abandoned princess journeys to underworld for healing water to save parents, becomes first mudang (shaman). Cha's version: not abandoned but loved child, sent by mother to well where mysterious woman gives magic medicine. 'Do not look back' motif. Arrives home at dusk — cure not confirmed.

Greek goddess of spring/underworld. Structural frame for ELITERE: incomplete return (pomegranate eaten = permanent bond to loss). 'Let the one who is daughter restore spring with her each appearance from beneath the earth.' (p.133). 'Until.' as grammar of unfinished waiting.

Greek harvest goddess. Searches 9 days/nights for daughter — parallel to Novena structure and to mother Huh Hyung Soon's waiting in exile. 'Let the one who is mother who waits nine days and nine nights be found.' (p.133).

Prophetess who sees truth but is not believed. Parallel to diseuse de bonne aventure (fortune-teller). Both speak truth that existing power structures refuse to hear. Connected to Spivak's 'Can the Subaltern Speak?'

Fictional character from Dreyer's film Gertrud (1964). Unhappy wife betrayed by husband. Left-page narrative in ERATO's split-screen structure. Her secular suffering mirrors Thérèse's sacred suffering on facing page. NOTE: fictional character — ontological class review pending (FRBRoo F38_Character may be more precise than Person).

Definition / Scope Note: 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988). Representational crisis: Vertreten (political proxy) vs Darstellen (portrayal). Framework for Diseuse's mediation and translational-violence concept.

'Mama's Baby, Papa's Maybe: An American Grammar Book' (1987). flesh/body distinction: enslaved women as 'female but not woman,' reduced to 'zero degree of social conceptualisation.' Ungendering concept. Primary theoretical source for dict:concept/ungendering — applied to URANIA's blood/ink transformation (pp.64-65).

'Coloniality of Gender' (2007); 'Toward a Decolonial Feminism' (2010). Gender itself as colonial introduction. Fractured Locus: active subjectivity between colonial designation and communal memory. Framework for shamanic mediation and cyclical time concepts.
'Under Western Eyes' (1984). 'Discursive colonisation': Western feminism constructs homogenised 'average third-world woman' as passive victim. Framework for anti-autobiography strategy.

'Unsettling the Coloniality of Being/Power/Truth/Freedom' (2003), CR: The New Centennial Review 3(3): 257-337. 'Overrepresentation of Man': Western bourgeoisie's mode of being presented as coterminous with Human. Man1 (rational political subject) → Man2 (bio-economic subject). Limitation: gender treated as biologically grounded — addressed by Spillers and Lugones.

Definition / Scope Note: 1919 Korean independence uprising against Japanese colonial rule. Yu Gwan-sun's participation and martyrdom. Temporal anchor: other events (1960, 1980) are 'recurrences' of this foundational structure of colonial violence.

1960 student uprising against Syngman Rhee. Brother's participation. 'De.Mo' (p.84): syllabic decomposition of Democracy as empty signifier. 'Dear Mother, 4.19. Four Nineteen... eighteen years later' (p.83).

1950-1953. Mother's Busan refuge. Cha born 1951 during war — birth itself as product of displacement. 'It is not 6.25. Six twenty five. June 25th 1950. Not today. Not this day.' (p.83). Negation as temporal invocation.

1980 pro-democracy movement brutally suppressed. Cha (age 29) returned to Korea, witnessed aftermath. 'Nothing has changed, we are at a standstill.' (p.87). Third iteration of national self-division after 1919, 1960.
1910-1945. Mother's language prohibition: 'They say you spoke in tongue forbidden' (p.45). Yu Gwan-sun's imprisonment and death. Structural context for translational violence across generations.

March 3, 1919. Mass gathering before March 1st Movement. Osaka Asahi Shimbun photograph (p.122) shows Koreans at memorial pavilion, Seoul. Photographic evidence of colonial-era mourning as political assembly.

1962. Mother and brother depart first; Cha (age 11-12) follows to Hawaii, then San Francisco. Defined as 'Exile' not 'Immigration' — forced departure triggered by brother's political activity. Sacred Heart Convent enrollment follows.

Critique of Western imperialism's subjugation of subjects through language and knowledge systems. Mohanty (1984) + Spivak (1988). Upper-level framework for entire Dictée analysis — all other theoretical concepts operate within this frame.

Intergenerational epistemic violence through forced linguistic assimilation. Mother (Huh Hyung Soon): Japanese enforced → Korean forbidden → Chinese ambient (Manchukuo). Cha: Korean suppressed → English enforced → French acquired (Sacred Heart). Spivak's epistemic violence materialized across two generations. Synthesis of Spivak (1988) + Fanon, Black Skin White Masks (1952) + Cha's text.

Authorial strategy of emptying self to channel absent voices — triadic structure: DISEUSE → Muses → Female Figures. 'She allows others. In place of her. Admits others to make full.' (p.3). Modeled on Korean mudang's 접신(接神) structure. NOTE: Modeling type — this is the researcher's interpretive frame, not a term in Dictée's text. Epistemological status must be explicitly argued in paper Section 5.

Definition / Scope Note: Spivak, Death of a Discipline (2003); Apter, The Translation Zone (2006). Impossibility of full semantic transfer between languages. Deliberate mistranslation, broken grammar, and silence as strategies exposing this impossibility. In Dictée: cygnes/signes (homophones in French, untranslatable to English); J'écoutais (imparfait, active listening) vs I heard (simple past, passive receipt) — each language preserves an untranslatable political remainder. The text refuses easy comprehension by Western readers.

Definition / Scope Note: Traditional Muses: passive inspiration for male artists, voiceless. Cha reclaims them as active channels for silenced women across colonial/gendered histories. Each Muse no longer represents single genre but unstable intersection of refugee, revolution, colonial education, martyrdom, shamanism. THALIA (Comedy) opens with MELPOMENE (Tragedy) fresco (p.138) — genre expectation deliberately violated.

9 chapters = 9-day Catholic devotional prayer (Novena). 'NOVENA: NINE EACH. THE RECITATION OR PRAYER AND PRACTICING OF DEVOTIONS DURING A NINE DAY PERIOD / And it begins.' (p.19). Catholic ritual + Greek myth + Korean shamanism = syncretic structural principle.

Ming dynasty (1341) Shisijing Fahui / Han dynasty Nanjing. Speech as physiological process. Tunstall: 'grief is located in the lungs' in Eastern medicine. Paired with vocal anatomy diagram — two knowledge systems approaching the same question.

Western anatomical cross-section of speech organs. Materialization of speech as bodily labor. Juxtaposed with Eastern meridian chart: two knowledge systems approaching the same question (how does the body produce speech?).

1919 Japanese police record card photograph. Colonial documentation repurposed as memorial icon. Also appears enlarged from group photo on back cover — Yu stands at right of back row (Ewha Hakdang students).
Circa 1940 photograph, age ~18. Also used in Cha's 1977 video Chronology — recurring maternal image across works. Placed at chapter opening as visual anchor for mother's diasporic narrative.
1904 photograph from French magazine La vie illustrée, showing Korean execution during Russo-Japanese War. Colonial violence documented and consumed by imperial media.
Korea with division line drawn across center. Visual evidence opening MELPOMENE chapter. 'She' = personification of divided peninsula. 'SHE opposes Her. SHE against her.' (p.87).

prefLabel (en): Thérèse as Joan of Arc Photo
Definition / Scope Note: 1895 photograph: Saint Thérèse costumed as Joan of Arc in play written for her sister. Identity layering: saint performs as martyr. Entry point for name chain: Cha(Theresa) → Thérèse → Joan → Falconetti → Gertrud.

prefLabel (en): Dreyer Joan of Arc Film Still
Definition / Scope Note: Still from La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc (1928). Falconetti's face in close-up. Silent woman in silent film — foreclosed speech visualized. Chapter's final image.

~27,000-year-old hand stencil, Spain. Part of Cha's ongoing project on 'representation of hands in Western painting' (Lee-Lenfield). Primordial mark-making. Connected to THALIA's 'Scratch. Marking. Uncontainable.' (p.150).

March 3, 1919 Japanese newspaper. Koreans gathered at memorial pavilion, Seoul, after Emperor Gojong's funeral. Colonial documentation as inadvertent archive of resistance. Facing page: 'Dead time' text.

Fresco of Melpomene (Tragedy) removing smiling mask to reveal unsmiling face. Comedy chapter (THALIA) opens with Tragedy's image — genre expectation deliberately violated. Key evidence for dict:concept/muse-subversion.

1857 Francis Frith photograph of Egyptian ruins along Nile. Ancient civilization as temporal depth — extends temporal stratigraphy beyond cave hand (27,000 years). NOTE: relationship to other concepts/objects not yet instantiated in File 5.

Definition / Scope Note: Cha Hyung Sang's brush calligraphy 女男 (Woman-Man) centered on pp.26-27. Gendered order reversed from conventional Korean 男女. Father's hand inscribes alternative gender grammar — connected to dict:concept/ungendering (subversion of colonial gender order).
Cha Hyung Sang's brush calligraphy 父母 (Father-Mother) centered on pp.54-55. Parental dyad as visual anchor in mother's narrative chapter.
Ten Daoist cosmic concepts including Taiji. Written in Chinese characters (p.154), Cantonese pronunciation transcribed in POLYMNIA (p.173). Cosmological framework for cyclical structure.
English cursive handwriting with visible deletions, line breaks. Editorial process made visible — composition as labor, not finished product. Materiality of writing exposed.
Korean folk song about separation from family and lost homeland. Embedded untranslated within English text — translational resistance through song. Connects to dict:concept/untranslatability.

'Period', 'Comma', 'Open quotation marks' written as words rather than symbols in dictation exercise. Language's regulatory infrastructure made visible. Diseuse 'would take on their punctuation... become, herself, demarcations.' (p.4). Connects to dict:rel/embodiesPunctuation.
Independent publisher, New York. Founded by Reese Williams. Cha worked as editor. Published Dictée (1982) and Apparatus (1981). Letterpress printing.
Published 2001 reprint/third edition of Dictée with BAMPFA. Returned book to print after 19 years out of print.

1980 video/film installation. Themes of exile and temporality shared with Dictée.
1980 video. Landscape and displacement. Manchurian/Mongolian geography of Cha family exile.
